analysis.one_liner: Freezes large agribusiness, food manufacturing, and grocery mergers until Congress rewrites antitrust rules for food markets.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee but never received a markup or floor vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned large mergers and acquisitions among big agribusiness firms, food and beverage manufacturers, and grocery retailers until Congress passed legislation the bill's authors considered comprehensive on food market concentration. It also would have created a 12-member commission to study concentration in meatpacking, seeds, grain, and grocery retail and recommend changes to antitrust law, with a $2 million budget and hearings in farming regions. The moratorium would apply to companies over roughly $160 million in sales or assets buying firms over $16 million, with an exception the Attorney General could grant only for financial distress.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers, who would gain a freeze on further consolidation among the handful of buyers they can sell to; rural communities dependent on farm economies; food and farm workers, whose wages the commission would study in connection with mergers; and shoppers, whose grocery prices the commission would examine against stagnant farm prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers, food workers, and shoppers

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a moratorium on mergers between large dealers, processors, agricultural input suppliers, brokers, and grocery retailers, blocking deals above roughly $160 million in sales or assets acquiring firms over $16 million, until comprehensive concentration legislation takes effect.

It creates a Food and Agriculture Concentration and Market Power Review Commission to study concentration's effects on farmers, workers, rural communities, and food shoppers, and to recommend changes to antitrust and related laws, reporting to Congress and the President within 12 months of its first meeting.

The commission's required study includes whether mergers cause wage suppression, layoffs, or reduced benefits for food and agricultural workers, and why low farm prices have not produced lower supermarket prices.

The commission must hold at least one hearing in Washington and four in different agriculture regions, must include farmers or ranchers among its members and a representative of organized labor among House-appointed members, and is barred from including current officers or employees of the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness firms, meatpackers, seed and agrichemical companies, food and beverage manufacturers, and big grocery retailers would bear the cost: they could not pursue large mergers or acquisitions while the moratorium is in effect, and would face a study of their market power with potential antitrust changes to follow. Taxpayers would fund the commission, authorized at $2 million.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large agribusiness, meatpackers, and grocery chains

drawbacks.text: The moratorium has no fixed end date: it lasts until the effective date of legislation that itself declares it 'comprehensive legislation' under the act, so a future Congress could keep the freeze in place indefinitely, and the Attorney General may waive it only for extraordinary circumstances such as insolvency.

A blanket ban on deals above the size thresholds would also block mergers that a case-by-case review would find harmless or even pro-competitive, and the insolvency-only waiver could leave distressed-but-not-bankrupt sellers without an exit.

The commission is a study body with no enforcement power; its $2 million appropriation and report would depend on a later Congress to act on its recommendations, so the bill's ultimate effect on concentration would be deferred.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a well-documented problem named in its own findings: a handful of firms now dominate meatpacking, seeds, grain trading, and grocery retail, farmers' share of the retail food dollar has fallen, and farm incomes have collapsed even as food prices rise. Its design favors caution over speed — an open-ended merger freeze rather than case-by-case review — which is a real cost for deals that would not harm competition. The commission structure also means the main antitrust changes would come later, not from this bill itself. But as a stop on further consolidation in markets where farmers and shoppers have few alternatives, the trade-off is weighted toward the public side.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Agriculture and Judiciary Committees and then to the Judiciary antitrust subcommittee, and neither committee took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, joined by Reps. DeLauro, Khanna, Pingree, Ryan, Blumenauer, and Schakowsky as original sponsors.

The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture and, in addition, to the House Committee on the Judiciary, for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
On June 28, 2019, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or Senate consideration, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Sixteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest meatpackers, seed and agrichemical companies, food manufacturers, and grocery chains are better off: the merger moratorium never took effect, so no new limits on consolidation were imposed, and no commission was created to examine their market power.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and all 16 cosponsors were House Democrats, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call shows how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The moratorium would have blocked large mergers among processors, and the commission would have studied packer ownership of livestock, contract growing, and barriers to entry in meatpacking — areas where a few firms buy from many farmers. The bill died, so these firms kept the freedom to consolidate.

The bill would have covered agricultural input suppliers in the merger freeze and directed the commission to study seed industry concentration, genetic diversity, and quadrupling corn seed costs. Its defeat preserved the merger options of the few large input firms.

industries.industry: Large grocery retailers and food and beverage manufacturers
industries.note: Grocery retailers and food manufacturers above the size thresholds would have been barred from large acquisitions, and the commission would have examined why supermarket prices stay high while farm prices fall. The bill's death left the sector's consolidation path unchanged.

The bill would have paused further consolidation of their buyers and sellers, and agricultural cooperatives are expressly excluded from the definitions, leaving co-ops free to combine. With the bill dead, farmers gained nothing and concentration continued without a federal review.
